p: Maria was on Highway 34 by 7:10, driving toward the hospital where she'd spent fourteen years of nights.

Greeley looked the same from the parking lot. Brick, a newer glass wing, the helipad, the smokers' bench that had been moved three times and still drew smokers. What was different was the lobby. Four people in business clothes stood by the information desk with laptops and lanyards, and the hospital president was shaking their hands with the smile of a man who had been told about them twenty minutes ago.

The Joint Commission doesn't call ahead. That's the point. Surveyors show up, ask for the census, pick patients, and follow their care through the building to see whether the hospital does what its policies say. They talk to nurses. They open cabinets. They ask a tech on the night shift where the fire extinguisher is and watch where the tech's eyes go.
Her phone buzzed while she was still in the car. Marcus. laramie queue still clean. digging into why nobody got paged. don't have it yet.
Then Kiran. When the backlog posted, the Laramie house supervisor texted the critical values to the nurses' cell phones. Just so you know before somebody else tells you.
Then Ochoa, who was apparently already at his desk. Greeley's yours for the week. Every tracer touches something you own. Don't hide anything and don't perform. Breakfast tomorrow, the diner, 6:30.

Maria sat in the car a minute longer. Three hours of lab results that nobody saw. Four surveyors who would spend the week looking for exactly that kind of gap. She had owned all of it for about a month.
She clipped on her badge and went in through the employee entrance, the way she always had.
Ochoa's Legal Pad: who makes the rules.

The diner was loud at 6:30 in the morning. Ochoa didn't seem to notice. He wrote four words down the side of his legal pad: law, regulation, accreditation, local. Everything that tells you what you can't do with a patient's information comes from one of these. Know which one you're looking at.

A law is passed by Congress or a state legislature. A regulation is the detailed rule a federal or state agency writes to carry out a law, and it has the force of law. Accreditation is voluntary, but most hospitals choose it: a private body like The Joint Commission surveys the hospital against its standards. Then there are state and local rules: licensing by the state health department, the state board of pharmacy, state privacy laws that can be stricter than federal ones, and state rules on how a health information exchange handles consent. HIPAA is a floor: a state law that protects privacy more than HIPAA isn't overridden by it.

The payers sit beside all of this. CMS runs Medicare and oversees Medicaid, which each state runs. CMS also writes the Conditions of Participation, the requirements a hospital has to meet to take Medicare and Medicaid patients at all. A hospital accredited by The Joint Commission can be deemed to meet them, which is why an unannounced survey makes a hospital president smile so hard.

How the exam asks it. Expect a question about who sets a requirement. Congress passes laws, agencies like CMS write regulations, accreditors like The Joint Commission survey against standards, and states license and add their own rules.
HIPAA is two rules and a bigger stick.

The HIPAA Privacy Rule covers protected health information, or PHI, in any form: paper, spoken, electronic. It says when a covered entity may use or disclose it. Covered entities are health plans, clearinghouses, and providers who send standard transactions, like claims, electronically. Treatment, payment, and health care operations don't need the patient's authorization. Many other uses need a written authorization, though the rule also allows some disclosures without one, like those required by law or for public health. The minimum necessary standard says use only what the job needs, though it doesn't apply when one provider sends information to another for treatment. The rule also gives patients rights: to see and get a copy of their records, to ask for corrections, to get an accounting of certain disclosures, to ask for restrictions, and to get a notice of privacy practices.

The HIPAA Security Rule covers electronic PHI only. It requires a risk analysis and three kinds of safeguards: administrative, like policies and training; physical, like locked server rooms; and technical, like access controls, audit logs, and encryption. Its goals are confidentiality, integrity, and availability. People forget the third one, Ochoa said. A chart nobody can open at three in the morning is a security failure too.

HITECH made HIPAA bite. It added the breach notification rule, made business associates, the vendors who handle PHI for you, directly liable, and raised the penalties. It also paid hospitals to adopt certified EHRs. Every vendor that creates, receives, keeps, or sends PHI on your behalf signs a business associate agreement.

How the exam asks it. Know which rule is which. Privacy covers all PHI and patient rights. Security covers electronic PHI and its safeguards. HITECH added breach notification and direct liability for business associates.
The rules that make data move.

For years the worry was data getting out. Now it's also data not getting where it should. The 21st Century Cures Act prohibits information blocking: a provider, a certified health IT developer, or a health information network or exchange may not interfere with access, exchange, or use of electronic health information unless a law requires it or an exception applies. The exceptions include preventing harm, privacy, security, and infeasibility. A blanket hold on test results so a doctor can call first isn't covered. A clinician's documented judgment that seeing it could endanger one specific patient's life or physical safety can be, and so can the patient's own request to wait.

Exchange runs on other rules too. ONC, now part of HHS's Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy office, certifies EHRs. TEFCA is a national framework that connects networks so records can follow patients across the country. Each HIE sets consent rules within state law, opt in or opt out. And 42 CFR Part 2 protects substance use disorder treatment records from federally assisted programs more tightly than HIPAA does. Recent changes let a patient sign one consent for treatment, payment, and operations, but the records still can't be used against the patient in a legal case without consent or a court order.
How the exam asks it. If a question describes a delay or a barrier to sharing records, think information blocking first, then ask whether an exception fits the specific patient.

EMTALA says a hospital with an emergency department that takes Medicare must give anyone who comes in a medical screening exam and stabilizing treatment, or an appropriate transfer, whether or not they can pay. Registration can't delay the screening to ask about insurance. Pharmacy has its own layer: state boards, pharmacist review of orders, and DEA rules that require two factor authentication to e-prescribe controlled substances. Environment of care covers the building itself: fire safety, utilities, and medical equipment. The Joint Commission now files these under Physical Environment. Emergency management standards sit beside them and cover what happens when the information systems go down. The FDA oversees software that works as a medical device.
And when the law's silent, Ochoa said, capping his pen, you do the ethical thing and write down why. Somebody will ask.
How the exam asks it. EMTALA questions usually hide inside a registration or downtime workflow. Any step that delays the screening exam to ask about payment is the wrong answer.
The first tracer went to the ICU. Of course it did. Maria followed the surveyor, a nurse from Ohio with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair, through doors she could have opened in her sleep.

Bev Hart was charge nurse. Bev had precepted Maria on her first night shift eighteen years ago and still called her "kid." The surveyor asked Bev a simple question. Your EHR goes down right now. How does a critical lab result reach you?
Bev opened her mouth and nothing came. Her eyes went to the shelf where the 2019 downtime binder used to be. It wasn't there. Then they went to Maria.
A. Tell the surveyor the downtime policy is being rewritten right now, so it's covered.
B. Step in and walk through the downtime process herself, so Bev doesn't look bad.
C. Let Bev answer, then tell the surveyor plainly what's missing and what she owns.
D. Suggest the surveyor trace a different patient, on the step down unit next door.

Bev says she'd call the lab and the lab would call her. That's half right. Afterward Maria tells the surveyor that the unit's downtime binder is missing, that her team owns the downtime procedures, and that a recent outage at another hospital showed the same gap. The surveyor writes for a long time. Bev squeezes Maria's arm in the hallway. You always did tell on yourself, kid.

That's the move. Accreditation exists to find exactly this. Let staff answer for themselves, then be honest about the gap and who owns it. A surveyor who finds a problem you already named sees a hospital that learns. One who finds a problem you hid sees a hospital that performs.
Decision two. Who owns the review.

At noon Maria took a call in a supply closet. The Laramie quality director wanted to know who was leading the review of last night. Three hours of delayed lab results, one critical potassium, no harm that anyone knew of yet.
I can write it up, Marcus said on the same call. It's my interface. Kiran offered to pull the list of every affected result. Everyone was helpful. Nobody was sure whose job it was.
A. Wait until the survey is over before opening a formal review of the Laramie event.
B. Lead the review herself, since clinical systems owns the interface and the outage.
C. Have Marcus write the review, since he knows the interface better than anyone.
D. File a safety event report and let patient safety lead, with IT on the team.

She files the report from the closet. The patient safety officer takes the lead by two o'clock and names a team: the Laramie lab, nursing, the house supervisor, Marcus for the technical cause, and Maria for the systems side. The review asks two questions: why it broke and why nobody knew. Marcus gets the first one.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Know who owns what. Patient safety and quality own the event review. IT owns the technical root cause and the fix. Clinical leaders own the downtime and callback practice. Reporting it through the event system is how the organization learns instead of just one department.
The Laramie house supervisor called back that afternoon. She sounded like she'd been up all night, because she had.
I texted the criticals to the nurses' personal phones. Name, room, value. I know. I'd do it again. It was faster than walking six units.
She wasn't wrong that it was faster. She also wasn't wrong that it put patient names on a dozen personal phones. Cascade's policy didn't say anything about downtime messaging at all.
A. Write a policy that bans PHI in any text message, with no exceptions at all.
B. Report the supervisor to HR for a violation, so other sites take it seriously.
C. Thank her, and let downtime texting stand as long as the phones are locked.
D. Write a downtime messaging policy with privacy and security, naming one secure channel.

Joan Whitfield, the privacy officer, and Nate Ostrowski, the CISO, meet with the house supervisor Thursday. The draft names the hospital's secure messaging app on unit phones as the only channel for PHI, keeps the phone callback for critical results, and spells out who verifies the values once the system is back. The house supervisor reads it and says, Okay. That I can do at 2 AM.

Exactly right. Security policy has three goals: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. A good downtime policy keeps urgent information moving, keeps it off devices you can't control, and makes sure what was sent gets checked against the record later.
At 8 PM the Greeley nurse manager for the medical floors caught Maria in the parking garage. Doug had a box of new downtime binders under one arm and a sheet of green stickers in his hand.
Printed twenty of these. I'll put one on every unit tonight. The stickers say reviewed. I figured I'd date them last spring, so it doesn't look like we scrambled.
He looked exhausted and proud of himself. He'd had a long day too.
A. Put the binders out tonight, but with today's date and no reviewed stickers.
B. Hold the binders back until the survey is over, so nothing looks rushed.
C. Thank him and let it go. The binders are real, and the dates are a small thing.
D. Tell him to ask the CNO, since unit documents are a nursing decision, not hers.

Doug winces, then laughs. Yeah. Okay. That was dumb. They put the binders out together, dated today. When a surveyor asks the next morning, the nurse says they came out last night, and she read hers. The surveyor nods.

That's the move. Fixing a gap fast is good. Faking when you fixed it isn't. Put the real fix in place, date it truthfully, and let the record show what actually happened. Honesty with an accreditor is an ethical duty, and it's also the better strategy.

Day two, the emergency department. The surveyor asked to see how the ED registers patients when Corvane is down. A registrar pulled the paper downtime form and walked through it with a made-up patient, a teenager with a broken wrist.
The paper form had been copied years ago from a registration screen two systems back. Insurance carrier and policy number were the first two boxes. The triage section was on the back.
The registrar did exactly what the form said and asked the pretend teenager about insurance first. The surveyor wrote it down.
A. Redesign the form so triage comes first and payment questions come after screening.
B. Move insurance to the back of the paper form, and leave the electronic build alone.
C. Explain to the surveyor that the paper form is rarely used, since downtime is rare.
D. Retrain the registrars to skip the insurance boxes until the nurse sees the patient.

She has a registration analyst pull the electronic quick registration build, and it has the same order. Both get fixed within the week with the ED director and compliance at the table: name, birth date, complaint, triage. Insurance after the medical screening exam starts.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. EMTALA requires a medical screening exam and stabilizing care regardless of ability to pay. Registration can go on in parallel, but asking about insurance can't delay the screening. Check both the paper downtime form and the electronic build, since they drift apart.
Aisha Rahman found Maria in the cafeteria at lunch, between tracers. Aisha was the CMIO, a hospitalist who moved fast and thought in data.

Quick favor. My fellow needs a de-identified extract for a sepsis study. All septic admissions, last two years, all eleven hospitals. No names, no MRNs. Just admit date, discharge date, ZIP code, age, labs, outcome. Can Kiran run it this week?
Maria looked at the list on the napkin. Admit dates. ZIP codes.
A. Run it as written, since no names or record numbers means it's de-identified.
B. Tell Aisha research data isn't a clinical systems job, and send it to the warehouse.
C. Call it what it is, a limited data set, and route it to Joan for an agreement.
D. Strip the dates and ZIP codes so it's fully de-identified, then run it today.

Aisha frowns, then nods. Fine. You're right, the dates are the whole study. Maria sends it to Joan Whitfield, the privacy officer, who sets up a data use agreement and checks the research approval. The fellow gets the extract in two weeks, legally.

Exactly right. Words matter. Data with dates and ZIP codes but no direct identifiers is a limited data set. It can be used for research under a data use agreement. Truly de-identified data has those removed too. Know the terms, and route each to the right owner.
Marcus called that evening with what sounded like good news. The regional HIE had noticed Laramie's feed went quiet during the outage, and while they were at it, they'd asked a question.

They want to move Cheyenne, Laramie, and Rawlins under Cascade's HIE agreement. Right now those three still send through the old MedaLink arrangement. I can repoint the feeds Friday. One problem. Rawlins has the behavioral health clinic, and its substance use treatment program. And MedaLink kept its own opt out list. I don't know what Cascade's agreement does with either.
It was a technical question on the surface. Maria knew it wasn't.
A. Hold the Rawlins clinic back, move the rest, and brief Joan once it's done.
B. Turn off the Wyoming feeds to the HIE until One Chart is live and settles it.
C. Repoint the feeds Friday. Better continuity of care is worth a few loose ends.
D. Bring Joan in first to map every consent rule before any of the feeds move.

Maria calls Joan Whitfield that night. Joan answers on the second ring and asks three questions Maria hadn't thought of. The plan they agree on carries the MedaLink opt out list into the new agreement, keeps the clinic's Part 2 records out unless a patient consents, and moves the feeds two weeks later than Marcus wanted.

That's the move. HIE consent depends on state law, the exchange's rules, the patient's recorded choice, and for substance use treatment, 42 CFR Part 2. That's a privacy decision. Bring the privacy officer in before you build, not after.
Day three. The Greeley medical staff president caught Maria after a meeting with a printed request signed by twenty-two physicians.
Patients see their lab results in the portal before we do. They panic and call at night. We want a seventy-two hour hold on every result before it releases. Your team can build that, right?
Her team could build it in an afternoon. That was the problem.
A. Hold only abnormal results, and release normal ones right away as they post.
B. Release on time, and let a clinician hold one result to protect a patient's safety.
C. Build the hold for all results, since the physicians have a real patient concern.
D. Turn off the portal's results release for now, until legal reviews the request.

Maria brings compliance and Joan into the room. Results release on time unless a law says otherwise. A physician can hold one specific patient's result after documenting that seeing it could endanger that patient's life or physical safety. Worry about a result isn't enough. Patients can choose to wait for a call. Kiran adds a portal note that says the doctor will follow up. The medical staff president isn't thrilled, but he signs it.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Information blocking rules expect results to reach patients without unnecessary delay. Exceptions exist, like preventing harm for an individual patient or a patient's own request to wait, but a blanket hold isn't one. Give clinicians tools to follow up with patients.
That afternoon her phone buzzed with a text.
A text from Joan Whitfield. Joan Whitfield, privacy. I hear Laramie had a rough night. Anything from it I should know about?

The spreadsheet was Kiran's list of every delayed Laramie result, with names, record numbers, and values. A Laramie lab analyst had emailed it to a personal account to work on at home. The analyst had told Kiran, and Kiran had told Maria, and Maria hadn't told anyone yet.
A. Have the analyst delete the email and the file, then remind the lab about policy.
B. Wait until the survey ends Friday, then bring the whole thing to Joan in one meeting.
C. Call Joan back now, share every fact, and let Joan run the breach assessment.
D. Ask Nate's team to check the account for forwarding before she brings it to Joan.

Joan listens without interrupting, then asks for the account type, the time, and whether the analyst forwarded it. The assessment takes two days. Joan handles the analyst with care. When it's done, Joan says, You called me before I had to call you. Keep doing that.

Exactly right. Report privacy events to the person who owns them, quickly and completely. The privacy officer decides, through a documented risk assessment, whether it's a reportable breach. Your job is facts and cooperation, and fixing whatever process let it happen.
By Thursday Maria had a draft plan to fix downtime procedures across Cascade. One binder template, one set of steps, one drill schedule, for every site.
Kiran read it and tapped one line. Home health nurses are in people's living rooms. They don't have a unit, or a binder shelf, or a lab down the hall. And the clinics close at five.
A. Leave home health and the clinics out, since the survey only covers the hospital.
B. Build procedures for each kind of site: hospital, critical access, clinic, and home.
C. Ask the vendors for their standard downtime kit and give that to every site.
D. Keep one template for everyone, and let each site adjust it locally as needed.

Home health gets offline visit notes on a tablet and a call tree. The clinics get a schedule printout at close of day. Rawlins, a critical access hospital with one IT tech, gets a simpler version Cheyenne will back up. It's four plans that share one spine.

That's the move. Different kinds of organizations deliver different services in different places. A home health agency, a clinic, a critical access hospital, and a referral center each need downtime procedures that fit how they actually work.
Thursday night Maria drafted an email to every clinical manager: from now on, all downtime procedures follow the attached steps. It felt good to write. She had her finger over Send.
Then she thought about the 2019 binder nobody could find, and the fact that nobody could tell her who had approved it.
A. Ask Ochoa to sign it as the CIO, so managers know it carries his authority.
B. Take it through policy review with an owner, approval, version, and review date.
C. Post it on the intranet as a guideline until the policy committee meets next month.
D. Send the email tonight. Speed matters, and the formal policy can catch up later.

She files it with the policy committee. The procedure gets a named owner, an approval path through nursing and IT, a version number, a review date a year out, and a training plan. The old 2019 version is formally retired so nobody finds it again.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Policies and procedures need governance: an owner, an approval path, version control, a place everyone can find them, training, and a review cycle. That's what makes them real at 3 AM and defensible in a survey.
Friday morning, the last day of the survey, a woman stopped Maria at the ICU desk. Her mother had been discharged to a rehab center in Loveland, and the rehab doctor wanted the records.

I'm her health care power of attorney. I have the paper. Medical records told me they can only print it, it's twenty-five cents a page, and it's eleven hundred pages. Can't you just put it on a flash drive?
She looked about forty. She had the same tired eyes Maria saw in the mirror after night shift. For a second Maria thought of Lucia, someday, standing at a desk like this one.
A. Verify her authority, then give an electronic copy at a reasonable cost-based fee.
B. Tell her HIPAA means only the patient herself can request copies of the records.
C. Give her the records now, since she's clearly family and it's for her mother's care.
D. Send the records directly to the rehab doctor, since that's a treatment disclosure.

Maria walks her to medical records, checks the power of attorney with the HIM manager, and asks why it has to be paper. There's no good reason. The daughter leaves with an encrypted electronic copy that afternoon. The HIM manager adds a note to fix the default.

Exactly right. Patients and their personal representatives have a right to access their records, in the electronic form they ask for if it's readily producible, for a reasonable cost-based fee. Verify identity and authority first. Paper only is a barrier, not a rule.

The exit conference was at three o'clock on Friday in the Greeley board room. Four surveyors at one end of the table, the hospital's leaders at the other, Ochoa in a chair along the wall like furniture, which was what he'd promised.
The lead surveyor read the summary in a flat, kind voice. Medication management, no findings. Infection control, no findings. Patient rights, no findings. Then she turned a page.

Preliminary finding: downtime procedures. The hospital does not consistently ensure that staff can carry out downtime procedures for its information systems. Downtime materials were missing or outdated on two units, and staff interviewed could not describe how critical results would reach them during an outage.
One finding. The hospital would stay accredited. And the one thing the surveyors had written up was the thing Maria owned.
Joan Whitfield, across the table, caught her eye and gave a small nod. It might have meant sorry. It might have meant good. With Joan, she was learning, it could mean both.

In the parking lot Ochoa walked her to her car. You told them before they found it, he said. They noticed. Now go find out why your hospitals didn't know their own procedures. Then fix that, not the binders.
Lucia was at the kitchen table when she got home, laptop open, a nursing school essay prompt on the screen. Describe a time a rule protected a patient. She'd written two sentences and deleted them.
Do you have one? she asked. A rule that actually saved somebody?

Maria thought about Bev's empty shelf, a pretend teenager with a broken wrist stuck behind an insurance question, a list of patients who'd said no to sharing. Most of the rules I know about, she said, sitting down, somebody got hurt first. That's how they got written.
Lucia looked at her for a long moment. That's kind of a sad essay, Mom. But she started typing.

It had been a hard week that went well. Maria had told the truth to a surveyor on her old unit and tried to put every problem in front of the person who owned it. None of that changed the finding. The finding was about the work before her, and now it was hers.
At 10:15 PM her phone lit up on the counter. Marcus. found why nobody noticed laramie. it's not the interface. you'll want to sit down for this one. tuesday?
